item.title: Professional surfer Arran Strong, 28, presumed dead after going missing of the coast of Portugal
item.description: Arran Strong, 28, vanished about a mile off Portugal's coast while crossing between beaches with his coach and is presumed dead after a four-day search.
item.content:encoded:
Professional surfer Arran Strong was presumed dead four days after going missing off the coast of Portugal in a tragic incident, the sports governing body in the UK confirmed.

The 28-year-old was a mile off the coast with his coach, Jose Maria Pyrrait, when the pair stopped to take a drink of water and take pictures. After taking a break for a few minutes, Pyrrait let Strong go ahead of him and then lost sight of him.

"In short: we stopped off Arrifana to drink water and take some pictures. We were there for a few minutes talking, when we started again," Pyrrait wrote in a post on Instagram. "I let him go ahead. Since my pace is faster. I always do that. When I would catch it and get a short lead I’d stop and wait for it."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"This time it was no different, but when I stopped to wait, I saw your board drifting about 100 meters away. I paddled as fast as I could to get there, diving repeatedly looking for it, but we were in a really deep area and visibility was very short."

Pyrrait said he immediately reached out to his partner on shore for help, and a local fisherman picked him up. They spent nearly 2 1/2 hours "scouring" the area for Strong using the boat’s sonar.

The Autoridade Marítima Nacional (AMN) told BBC Sport it was alerted to Strong having difficulties in the water at 11:33 BST Monday.

"The young man disappeared at sea while crossing from Monte Clerigo Beach to Carrapateira," the AMN told the outlet.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"His friend, who was with him, was rescued by a local fishing boat that was nearby."

The AMN confirmed that its search for Strong was halted Thursday. Pyrrait said Strong was like a "son" to him in his heartbreaking post.

"Arran was like a son to me; he had been training with me and spending weekends and holidays with me since he was ten years old—as I used to tell his mother, he was like the child of divorced parents. I loved him as if he were another son life had given me," Pyrrait wrote.

"Curiously, he always used to say he would die young. Right now, I feel profound pain; my only faint consolation is that he passed away at sea—a place he loved so dearly. He was young, with a pure and good heart, but he is gone. I feel empty and weary, yet life goes on."

Strong was the highest-ranked British surfer when he competed for Great Britain in each of the last two World Surfing Games. He competed in the World Surf League for a decade.

GB Surfing released a statement on the "tragic passing" of Strong Tuesday.

"Arran proudly represented Great Britain at the 2024 and 2025 ISA World Surf Games, finishing as our highest-placed male surfer on both occasions. Beyond his performances in the water, Arran was a fantastic teammate, respected competitor and a kind, generous presence whose passion for surfing left a lasting impression on everyone who had the privilege of knowing him," the statement said.

"His passing is a devastating loss to our sport and the wider surfing community, and he will be greatly missed. Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with Arran’s family, friends, teammates and all those whose lives he touched."

item.title: Brittney Griner files for divorce from wife of 7 years who fought for her release from Russia
item.description: Brittney Griner filed for divorce from Cherelle Griner, who helped get the WNBA star out of a Russian prison, saying the marriage is "irretrievably broken."
item.content:encoded:
WNBA player Brittney Griner has filed for divorce from her wife of seven years, Cherelle, court records show.

Cherelle was a vocal voice during Griner's Russian imprisonment, constantly pleading with U.S. government officials to bring the former Atlanta Dream star home.

When Griner returned home in late 2022, she thanked then-President Joe Biden for his efforts.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

"Over the last 9 months you have been so privy to one of the darkest moments of my life and so today I’m just standing here overwhelmed with emotions but the most important emotion that I have right now is just sincere gratitude for President Biden and his entire administration," Cherelle said with Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris by her side.

Cherelle thanked several members of the Biden administration, Griner's former Phoenix Mercury, the WNBPA and Brittney’s agency for doing all they could to keep the WNBA superstar in the spotlight after she was detained, sentenced and then transferred to a Russian penal colony in the final moments of her detention.

"Today, my family is whole. But as you all are aware," Cherelle added. "There are so many other families who are not whole. BG’s not here to say this, but I will gladly speak on her behalf and say that BG and I will remain committed to the work on getting every American home, including Paul (Whelan) whose family is in our hearts today as we celebrate BG being home. We do understand that there’s still people out here who are enduring what I endured the last 9 months of missing, tremendously, their loved ones."

The Griners married in 2019 and share a son, but the WNBA star, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported, said the marriage was "irretrievably broken."

WNBA SUDDENLY WANTS TO STICK TO BASKETBALL AFTER YEARS OF MAKING POLITICS PART OF THE PRODUCT

Griner was freed in a prisoner exchange for convicted Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout. She was arrested at Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow on Feb. 17, 2022, after Russian authorities said she had vape cartridges with cannabis oil inside her luggage. On Aug. 4 of that year, Griner was given a nine-year sentence after pleading guilty, arguing that she had been prescribed cannabis for her pain and inadvertently packed it. Her sentence was upheld in October, and she was later transferred to a penal colony.

Bout is known as the "Merchant of Death" and the possible swap for him was floated back in May. He was in the middle of a 25-year sentence in federal prison after he was convicted of conspiracy to kill Americans relating to the support of a Colombian terrorist organization.

Griner wrote in her memoir that she expected Cherelle to get a divorce if she had actually stayed in Russia for her entire prison sentence.

"My basketball career would be over. I’d be in my early forties and out of shape, would have to find a new way to provide for my wife. And Relle. She assured me she’d wait, but ten years was ridiculous," Griner wrote, via Complex.

"I went through so many emotions being locked up, and just thinking about nine years," she continued. "We planned on having kids, and doing all these amazing things together, and now I'm thinking, ‘Is that going to happen? How can I ask her to wait?’"

This would be Griner's second divorce. Griner married then-fellow WNBA star Glory Johnson in May 2015, despite both being arrested on charges of domestic violence against one another just three weeks prior. Johnson announced the following months she was pregnant via IVF and a sperm donor, and Griner filed for divorce the next day. That divorce was finalized June 2016.

Griner filed for the divorce on Thursday, and a hearing is slated for Sept. 1. She now plays for the Connecticut Sun.

Fox News' Ryan Gaydos contributed to this report.

item.title: American Red Cross declares national blood crisis as type O supply drops to dangerous levels
item.description: The American Red Cross declared a blood crisis across the nation as donations hit a four-year summer low, forcing limits on type O blood distributions to hospitals.
item.content:encoded:
The American Red Cross has declared a "blood crisis" across the nation.

The organization released a warning about the second-ever blood supply crisis this week after blood donations fell to a four-year summer low.

This decline worsens an emergency shortage that "threatens the availability of lifesaving blood for patients across the country," the organization wrote in a press release.

MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY

The Red Cross is now limiting distributions of type O blood to hospitals, as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products now has less than a one-day national supply of type O positive blood.

Type O blood accounts for about 60% of Red Cross blood distributions and is essential for both everyday patient care and medical emergencies.

Type O positive is the most commonly transfused blood type, according to the Red Cross, and can be safely given to about 80% of patients. 

Type O negative remains the universal blood type "relied upon when every second counts."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

While thousands of Americans show up to donate blood, these donations are reportedly not keeping up with hospital demand during summer trauma season.

This summer’s conditions, amid extreme heat, poor air quality and foodborne illnesses, have contributed to lower donor turnout, the Red Cross reported. Other blood collectors have also reported critical shortages this summer.

The Red Cross advised that just three more donors at each blood drive can end the crisis and stabilize the blood supply.

It encourages Americans to book an appointment by using the Blood Donor App, visiting RedCrossBlood.org, or by calling 1-800-RED CROSS (1-800-733-2767).

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Chris Hrouda, president of Red Cross Biomedical Services, shared information about the developing emergency in a statement.

"The Red Cross takes its responsibility as the nation’s largest single provider of blood products incredibly seriously and has worked tirelessly to strengthen the blood supply for our hospital partners," he said.

Following the organization’s first national blood crisis in January 2022, Hrouda said the Red Cross has put "additional safeguards" in place to help "prevent a crisis like that from happening again."

"But this summer, blood donations simply are not keeping pace with hospital demand, and inventories — especially type O blood — remain under significant strain," he said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Every donation has the potential to help save lives, and we urgently need everyone who is eligible to make an appointment to give blood as soon as possible."

item.title: Washington Post opinion editor to exit paper after just one year, staff completely 'blindsided'
item.description: A source says Post leadership was "blindsided" by Adam O'Neal's exit after he reshaped the opinion section to champion free markets and liberties.
item.content:encoded:
Washington Post opinion editor Adam O'Neal announced his exit from the paper on Friday after roughly just one year on the job.

"I’m writing to announce that I have decided to leave The Washington Post. My last day will be August 31," O'Neal told staff in a memo obtained by Fox News Digital.

"I joined The Post to lead the opinion section as it began a new chapter, and we have made dramatic changes over the past year. We quickly embraced our mission of championing free markets and personal liberties while simultaneously putting Post Opinions on a sustainable footing. Our work has become more relevant, accessible and consequential. We regularly publish world-class journalism that finds the audience where it is," O'Neal wrote before touting improvements in the opinion section's page views and time spent on the site.

EDITORIAL OVERHAUL: WASHINGTON POST'S NEW OPINION CHIEF FEELS THE WEIGHT OF THE CHALLENGES AHEAD

"I want to thank Jeff Bezos, Jeff D’Onofrio and the entire leadership team. And I especially want to thank everyone in Post Opinions. It has been an honor to have worked with such exceptional people at such an exceptional institution. While this was not an easy decision, I am leaving proud of how far the opinion section has come and optimistic that its best days lie ahead," he added.

Jeff D’Onofrio, The Washington Post's acting CEO and publisher, thanked O'Neal and crediting him for making the opinion section "more balanced in perspective, more financially sustainable and more accessible to readers than ever before," adding that a leadership transition will be in the works leading up to his Aug. 31 departure.

JEFF BEZOS REPORTEDLY TOLD TRUMP THE WASHINGTON POST WAS HIS ‘WORST INVESTMENT’ BEFORE STAFF CUTS

A source familiar with O'Neal's exit told Fox News Digital that Post leadership was "blindsided" by the decision and there were no tensions between him and D’Onofrio and owner Jeff Bezos.

O'Neal held an all-hands meeting with staff where he revealed it was a "personal decision" to leave The Post and that everyone in the room was "incredibly surprised," according to a staffer who attended the meeting.

O'Neal did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

JEFF BEZOS' TENURE AS WASHINGTON POST OWNER IN SPOTLIGHT AS PAPER GRAPPLES WITH LOW MORALE, STAFFER EXODUS 

O'Neal joined The Post last July after serving as a correspondent for the British outlet The Economist and as an editorial page writer for The Wall Street Journal. He was tasked to carry out Bezos' directive that The Post's editorial pages would promote "personal liberties and free markets," something that sparked intense backlash among both staffers in the newsroom and liberal critics. 

Bezos' edict led to the immediate resignation of O'Neal's predecessor, David Shipley. 

In his first interview as The Post opinion editor, O'Neal told Fox News Digital in September he felt "a tremendous responsibility to get this right."

"Our readers are overwhelmingly liberal, right?" O'Neal conceded. "And they're all overwhelmingly located in blue states. And just a few blue states. And they're over-represented on the coasts. And so, one way to look at it would be to say, 'Well, if you're non-partisan, and you have a highly partisan readership, they may be offended by that.' And maybe that's true. But looking forward as I rebuild, I really just see it as an opportunity to expand our reach."

He continued, "And frankly, a lot of people don't trust The Post. And they don't trust the mainstream media more broadly. And so my mission is to hire the kinds of people from throughout the U.S. with different kinds of backgrounds, intellectual diversity, who can appeal and rebuild that trust. And I think that a lot of folks have a poor view of The Post because they don't feel that they've been well served by it."

item.title: Michigan hospital pays $410K to settle lawsuit by physician assistant fired over transgender policy
item.description: Valerie Kloosterman says she was fired three weeks after requesting a religious accommodation from mandatory gender identity training at the hospital.
item.content:encoded:
A Michigan hospital has agreed to pay $410,000 to settle a lawsuit brought by a physician assistant who said she was fired after refusing to comply, due to her faith convictions, with workplace policies related to transgender patients, according to court filings and statements from the parties.

Valerie Kloosterman sued University of Michigan Health-West after she was terminated in August 2021.

"All I wanted to do was provide the best care possible to my patients without being forced to violate my Christian beliefs," Kloosterman said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

CHRISTIAN SCHOOL CHAPLAIN WINS SETTLEMENT AFTER FIRING OVER LGBTQ SERMON

First Liberty Institute, which represents Kloosterman, said she had received positive performance reviews throughout her employment before raising faith-based objections to mandatory gender identity training.

The organization told Fox News Digital Kloosterman was fired three weeks after requesting a religious accommodation from finishing a mandatory training that required her to affirm statements about gender identity that were in violation of her Christian faith.

According to First Liberty Institute, UMHW made no effort to accommodate her beliefs. She sued in October 2022.

CHRISTIAN LIFEGUARD WHO REFUSED PRIDE FLAG DUTIES AND WAS SUSPENDED IS NOW HEADED TOWARD TRIAL

The lawsuit says University of Michigan Health-West officials called her to a meeting, where they disparaged her religious beliefs, called her "evil" and a "liar," told her she could not bring her Christian beliefs into the workplace, and accused her of contributing to suicides among individuals with gender dysphoria.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

The settlement, according to the legal group, calls for UMHW to make a religious accommodation policy that complies with the law, inform and train all employees, give reasonable religious accommodations without retribution to those who request it, and pay the $410,000 in damages and fees to Ms. Kloosterman and her attorneys.

"This new policy ensures that providers of faith and employees at UMHW will receive religious accommodations so that they can provide excellent care consistent with their medical judgment, because all patients are created in the image of God," Kloosterman said in her statement to Fox News Digital.

GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS

"Title VII prohibits employers from discriminating against and punishing employees for their faith," Kayla Toney, counsel at First Liberty, said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "Valerie is an exceptional physician assistant who cares for each of her patients. Employers cannot drive out people like Valerie just because of their sincere religious beliefs. We are grateful to have resolved this matter with University of Michigan Health-West."

Fox News Digital reached out to University of Michigan Health-West for comment.

item.title: Fauci faces lifetime ban from federal government work under new bill following explosive hearing
item.description: Rep. Rich McCormick's bill could ban Anthony Fauci from federal employment after he invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times before Rand Paul.
item.content:encoded:
A House GOP proposal would bar Dr. Anthony Fauci from working for the federal government again after his dramatic hearing on Capitol Hill this week.

Fauci appeared before the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., where he invoked the Fifth Amendment over 100 times.

Republicans have been hammering the former public health official over the move, and now a new bill by Rep. Rich McCormick, R-Ga., would bar him from returning to his old duties and potentially open him to criminal prosecution.

RAND PAUL SEEKS CONTEMPT CHARGES AFTER FAUCI INVOKES FIFTH AMENDMENT MORE THAN 100 TIMES

"We saw him evade so many questions, pleading the Fifth... that's fine, that's your constitutional right," McCormick said in a video shared with Fox News Digital. "But you also have the right, if your till comes up short at Burger King, when your boss asks you why are you short $20 in your cash register — if you plead the Fifth, that's your... ability, but I can fire you."

He argued, "It should be the same way in government. If you don't want to answer questions about what you did wrong, we should be able to fire you."

The bill, called the STOP the SWAMP Act, would bar people from working for the federal government if they refuse to answer certain questions from federal lawmakers or if they are convicted of perjury, according to a news release on McCormick's website.

EXCLUSIVE: BIDEN PARDON WON'T SHIELD FAUCI IF HE LIES TO CONGRESS, COMER SAYS

It would also authorize members of Congress to refer hearing witnesses for prosecution if they were found to have unlawfully withheld information from lawmakers, the release said.

Fauci is not currently facing any criminal charges and has consistently denied any wrongdoing. But Paul, a longtime critic of Fauci's, said his committee would begin the process for holding the doctor in contempt of Congress after the hearing.

Fauci appeared before the Senate GOP-led panel on Wednesday amid new scrutiny over how he handled the COVID-19 pandemic, following the release of a diary he kept during the global health crisis.

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Diary entries made public by Paul ahead of the hearing showed the high-profile doctor reflecting on his pandemic-era fame and discussing the disease's origins.

Some entries appeared to show Fauci taking credit for influencing policies that closed schools during the pandemic, one of the most hotly debated aspects of how the government handled COVID.

He told the House Oversight Committee in January 2024, however, "I did not close the schools."

The longtime doctor became the public face of the U.S. government's COVID-19 response and drew both praise and criticism.

He previously served as director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases from 1984 to 2022.

item.title: Internet erupts over report that Platner's replacement in key Senate race fathered children with second cousin
item.description: Troy Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner on the Maine ballot, fathered two children with his second cousin, sparking fierce social media reaction.
item.content:encoded:
Conservatives lit up on Thursday night in response to a report claiming that Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson, who recently replaced disgraced candidate Graham Platner on the ballot, fathered two children with his second cousin and high school sweetheart.

The report, from Maine Wire editor-in-chief Steve Robinson, found that Jackson shares two adult sons with a woman named Lana Pelletier, his second cousin with whom he shares the same great-grandparents.

The report pointed out that the relationship is not uncommon in northern rural Maine, where Jackson is from, and that it is not illegal, but many on social media reacted with shock and criticism.

"Can’t wait for Democrats to defend cousin marriage!," Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., posted on X.

MAINE DEM IN HOT SEAT FOR CHAMPIONING POPULAR VOTE DESPITE CLINCHING SENATE BID WITHOUT IT

"If you thought Platner was a freak - meet Troy Jackson," former White House press secretary Sean Spicer posted on X.

KAMALA HARRIS BACKS US SENATE CANDIDATE WHO REPLACED GRAHAM PLATNER: 'I KNOW WHAT IT IS LIKE'

In a post on X, Independent Women's Forum Senior Policy Analyst Inez Stepman wrote, "*Second* cousins seem like relevant information here. But it is funny that Dems keep selecting candidates who fit the vicious stereotypes they hold about rural or working-class people: beats women, hooks up with cousin, etc."

"It's truly hysterical how Democrats can't seem to find one normal dude to run for office," conservative commentator Greg Price posted on X.

The Republican account on X also posted, "Wellness check on Maine Democrats."

In a statement to Fox News Digital, the Jackson campaign said, "Susan Collins will do anything to distract from the fact that she votes with Trump 96% of the time and has sold out working people in Maine. Personal attacks on Troy's family are shameful and desperate."

Jackson, a former state senator who ran unsuccessfully in the Democratic Maine gubernatorial primary this year, was tapped as the U.S. Senate nominee at the Maine Democratic Party's U.S. Senate Nominating Convention earlier this month.

Graham Platner, who won the 2026 Maine Democratic U.S. Senate primary last month, dropped out of the race earlier this month in the face of a rape allegation, though he had asserted, "Any accusation of non-consensual behavior is categorically false."

The general election, where Jackson will square off against incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins, will be on Nov. 3, as Republicans attempt to hold on to their 53-47 majority in the Senate.

item.title: Country singer Ruston Kelly commits to sobriety after relapsing on drugs following freak golf cart crash
item.description: Ruston Kelly reveals he relapsed after a golf cart accident left him with a broken arm and a month-long Percocet prescription that spiraled quickly.
item.content:encoded:
Ruston Kelly surrendered to sobriety after a freak accident nearly derailed his life.

Kelly, 37, admitted he was three days sober after relapsing following a golf cart crash in June.

The country music singer reflected on the last few challenging months in a candid social media post shared Wednesday with followers.

'BAYWATCH: HAWAII' STAR BRANDY LEDFORD SAYS SHE 'WANTED TO TRULY CHECK OUT' BEFORE REHAB SAVED HER LIFE

Kelly showed fans a gold Narcotics Anonymous token which read, "My gratitude speaks when I care and when I share with others the NA way." Recovery chips are often shared in meetings to commemorate clean living milestones.

"I told myself back in 2021 that as long as I wasn’t using amphetamines that I would be on the right 'clean' journey for myself," Kelly shared on Instagram. "I had never been addicted to any drug other than those pills. I lumped in alcohol and THC etc initially because I thought that’s what I was supposed to do."

"Somewhere along the way I became obstinate in my journey, that I wasn’t an 'addict' in the traditional sense of the word, that I was only addicted to amphetamines. 'I’ve never had a problem with alcohol, I’ve never had a problem with XYZ.' 'See I can be like everyone else, I can show self control, I am in control.'"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Despite reaching a point of "spiritual surrender," Kelly admitted he was only attempting to "live a lifestyle that was satisfactory to my carnal impulses because I 'never had a problem with them.'"

APP USERS CLICK HERE TO VIEW POST

In June, Kelly broke his arm "in half" following a golf cart accident where he overcorrected the vehicle and flipped the cart.

"After my accident where I broke my arm in half, I was given fentanyl morphine ketamine dilaudid and oxycodone for 3 days leaving with a month long Rx of Percocet," Kelly wrote. "I needed it for the level 15 pain but very quickly they started running out sooner and sooner.

"I was chewing them in the pharmacy before I walked out the door. I was hiding how many at a time I was taking. I was complaining to the dr it wasn’t enough."

His new drug dependency "awakened something I hadn’t felt in a very long time."

"On July 26 I decided to end any chance of ruining anything good," Kelly confessed. "For my soul my wife my family my art and career and my people. I admitted that whether I like it or not I will forever have a substance abuse disease."

He added, "ALL drugs/substances including alcohol and THC are off the table for good (working on nicotine) That if there is something that will scratch an itch I didn’t think I had, I will use it beyond excess and into addiction.

"I am 3 days completely clean and sober again, and intend to remain this way forever, one day at a time."

item.title: Top Wisconsin Democratic socialist candidate confronted on past 'defund police' rhetoric
item.description: Francesca Hong confirmed her DSA membership since 2020 but says her views on police abolition have evolved since her earlier social media posts.
item.content:encoded:
Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial frontrunner Francesca Hong defended her active membership in the Democratic Socialists of America while attempting to distance herself from some of its most extreme proposals Friday.

Speaking on "America’s Newsroom," Hong was confronted over previous posts endorsing far-left causes like abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), dismantling the Senate and defunding the police. Her appearance came a month after she appeared on Hasan Piker’s broadcast, where she defended many of the DSA’s policies.

Fox News’ Dana Perino questioned whether there was anything Hong disagreed with regarding the DSA platform, to which she responded that abolishing the Senate is "nonsensical and non-practical at this time." She also rejected their platform of getting rid of the Supreme Court, citing a belief in checks and balances.

DEMOCRATIC WISCONSIN GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE DOESN'T RECALL 'ABOLISH THE SENATE' POST IN 2021, CAMPAIGN SAYS

Perino then asked directly whether Hong was personally a dues-paying member of the socialist organization.

"In my home chapter in Madison, I have been since 2020," Hong confirmed, describing herself as a "democratic socialist," "a good single mom" and a "service industry worker."

However, Perino pressed Hong on past social media posts where she repeatedly called for police abolition, asking: "Why shouldn't people take you at your word when you say that you want to defund the police and go towards abolishing it?"

WISCONSIN DEM SOCIALIST GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL DODGES WHETHER SHE STILL WANTS TO ‘ABOLISH POLICE’

Hong said her views had evolved, replying, "I believe that people can evolve. We meet Trump voters from previous elections who now would like to vote for me."

"So who needs to evolve, the voter or you?" Perino asked. Hong then rejected her previous position, noting that the governor of Wisconsin would be unable to defund the police, and promising that if elected she "won’t defund the police."

The focus on the DSA’s platform has highlighted a rift in the Democratic Party, as many moderate Democrats reject its policies, despite several DSA candidates notching primary wins, including in New York and Colorado.

In June, Hong appeared on Piker’s stream, where she confirmed aspects of her platform, including supporting universal childcare, free school meals, abolishing ICE, public grocery stores and legalizing cannabis, among others.

Polling has Hong poised to take the Democratic nomination for Wisconsin governor, despite frequently being pressed by outlets about her past statements online. She has been backed by local Wisconsin DSA chapters and has gotten public support from key Democratic figures, including Reps. Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna.

FORMER CLINTON OFFICIAL WARNS 'RADICAL' SOCIALIST TAKEOVER WILL 'DESTROY' THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IF UNCHECKED

Hong called for abolishing police in a 2021 social media post after federal prosecutors chose not to charge the officer accused of shooting Jacob Blake, a Black man, in Kenosha. She addressed those comments in a May statement to Fox News Digital but did not say then whether she continued to support abolishing the police.

"There is no way I want to cut resources for public safety," Hong said. "I don’t like crime. I don’t like unsafe streets. I also don’t like when a member of law enforcement abuses their power."

Her campaign also previously addressed her "Abolish the Senate" comments, noting she did not recall making the post in 2021, which came after the Senate failed to convict President Donald Trump during impeachment proceedings.

Fox News’s CJ Womack contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump blasts Spain migrant surge as 'catastrophe,' warns US could face worse if Democrats regain power
item.description: President Donald Trump said during a Cabinet meeting that similar scenes of migrants flooding into Spain could play out in the U.S. if Democrats gain power.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump said Friday during a Cabinet meeting that scenes of migrants flooding into Spain's enclave of Ceuta from Morocco looked like a "catastrophe," but that the U.S. could see worse in the future if Democrats regain power.

"You know, I saw Spain yesterday, and I watched the catastrophe that took place. It looks like an invasion of a country by hundreds of thousands of people. And that same thing is going to happen to us if the Republicans don't get elected," Trump said Friday at Camp David. "Except worse, much bigger, much easier to get into. Despite the fact that we have built thousands of miles of wall, which I said we were going to do. But if we didn't have that, forget it. But we have the safest border in the world. If we're not in office, our country will be invaded at levels that made Spain look small time."

"And when I watched it, I said, boy, I said, ‘I'm going to say it because I knew you were going to be at Camp David.’ And I say, ‘That's going to be a talking point for the midterms, because when you look at what happened to Spain, they don't know what to do.’ And it's happening again today," the president continued. "They're coming in by the tens of thousands. It’s just invading the country. And what that is weak law, bad management, but very liberal law. They passed a couple of laws and people read, you know, people are smart. They read from other countries, and they swam that three-mile swim or however they got in."

"But nobody's seen anything like it. That will look good compared to what's going to happen to the United States," Trump also said. WHITE HOUSE BLASTS SPANISH GOVERNMENT AS THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS SURGE FROM MOROCCO, EMERGENCY REQUEST DENIED

U.S. border security has remained a key plank of the president's campaign and policy focus throughout his political career.

An English translation of a Friday Spanish-language post on X from Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said, "The Government will guarantee the safety of the residents of Ceuta, intensifying the presence of the Security Forces and Corps on the city's streets." FIREBRAND REP UNLOADS ON SOCIALIST PRIME MINISTER AS 'HORDES OF MILITARY AGED MEN' SWARM EUROPEAN COUNTRY

Ceuta, which is located along the northwestern African coast and borders Morocco, is not attached to mainland Spain.

We will expedite the repatriation files of the migrants who arrived irregularly. Around 60,000 migrants had ventured from Morocco to Ceuta over the past 24 hours, Cueta President Juan Jesús Vivas said on Friday.

At least 41 migrants lost their lives.

SPAIN DEPLOYS MILITARY AFTER THOUSANDS OF MIGRANTS OVERWHELM BORDER ENCLAVE, AT LEAST 18 DEAD

Many young Moroccans who crossed into Ceuta told The Associated Press that they had hoped to find better work opportunities in Spain but were returning given the mayhem in Ceuta.

"There’s nothing at home. I’d have to work 12-hour shifts for a meager wage. That’s why I came here," said 21-year-old Abdulah Buji, who hails from the city of Tetouan. "But I haven’t found any opportunities here either, so I have to go back."

Moroccan police used water cannons and fired warning shots into the air to prevent migrants from crossing into Ceuta, according to rights groups in Morocco.

Authorities in Ceuta and Madrid have linked the border surge to a recent decision by the Spanish Supreme Court, which ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, unlike those who cross by land or climb the border fence.

Sánchez said migrant smugglers misinterpreted the ruling.

The interpretation of the Supreme Court’s ruling "spread like wildfire over the past few hours through the networks of human trafficking organizations," triggering the surge, Sánchez said.

The Spanish Interior Ministry issued its own numbers not long after Vivas spoke, estimating that some 50,000 individuals had come from Morocco since Thursday. It noted that 37,500 had already returned, with hundreds of others heading back to Morocco by the hour.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Trump rejects Iran blame for Minnesota cyberattack, points finger at 'corrupt' political foe
item.description: Trump dismissed claims that Iranian hackers targeted Minnesota water systems, instead blaming the state's governor for what he called gross incompetence.
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump dismissed speculation that Iran was behind a cyberattack targeting dozens of water systems in Minnesota, blaming instead the state’s "corrupt governor," Tim Walz, and the state he runs.

"I just want to mention that we heard in Minnesota there was a cyberattack, and they blame it on Iran," he said at the start of a Cabinet meeting Friday at Camp David, Maryland.

"I don't think so. I think I blame it on Minnesota because they're grossly incompetent," Trump said. "There was a cyberattack of 30 water plants, and I would blame it on Minnesota and the governor, the corrupt governor of Minnesota. They like to say, oh, is Iran? Iran should be so lucky. Iran's got bigger problems than worrying about Minnesota."

Trump’s dismissal puts him at odds with a preliminary assessment reportedly shared by U.S. and state officials and comes days after federal agencies warned that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the same kinds of systems. Iranian involvement and poor cybersecurity are not mutually exclusive: previous Iranian-linked attacks on U.S. water facilities exploited internet-connected equipment protected by default or nonexistent passwords.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBES MINNESOTA OVER 'TRANSGENDER DOLLS' IN SCHOOLS, BUT STATE DISPUTES STORY

Waltz shot back in a post on X: "Trump knows exactly who is responsible for this attack, and knows that other states were hit too. This is what modern warfare looks like, and it further illustrates there’s no plan to win a war with Iran."

Trump repeatedly has attacked 2024 vice presidential candidate Walz over widespread fraud in Minnesota’s state-administered social services programs.

Walz, the 2024 Democratic vice presidential nominee, abandoned his bid for a third term in January amid mounting scrutiny of his administration’s handling of the schemes. Walz has not been accused of participating in the fraud.

Minnesota IT Services said the "coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 Minnesota community water systems" Sunday and Monday, but the Minnesota Department of Health is "not aware of any active requests from Minnesota cities to have their residents modify their drinking water usage."

U.S. and state officials and others familiar with the incident told The New York Times that Iranian hackers were likely behind the cyberattack.

Minnesota IT Services said it has not determined yet whether a "specific actor" was responsible for the attack and the probe remains active.

The attacks disrupted automated operations in several communities.

Malicious software temporarily shut down controls for the well and water treatment plant in Braham, while Plymouth and South St. Paul shifted some operations to manual control. Officials reported no known threat to drinking water.

Federal agencies warned just days before the Minnesota attacks that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting the computerized controls used by water systems, power facilities and local governments. The agencies said the campaign had already disrupted operations at some facilities and caused financial losses. Investigators assessed that the hackers were seeking to cause disruption inside the U.S.

Iran has targeted American water infrastructure before.

In 2023, hackers affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps breached programmable controllers at several U.S. water and wastewater facilities, according to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

The hackers generally exploited equipment that was exposed to the internet and still used default or nonexistent passwords. The affected utilities moved some operations offline, and no drinking water was compromised.

In an earlier case, the Justice Department charged an Iranian hacker with repeatedly accessing the control system of a small dam in Rye, New York, in 2013. Prosecutors said the intrusion would have allowed him to operate the dam’s sluice gate remotely, but the gate had been manually disconnected for maintenance at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

Fox News' Gregory Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

item.title: Keep your eyes trained on this Big Ten sleeper to make some conference noise in 2026
item.description: Jedd Fisch's Washington Huskies rank in the top 15 in returning production with quarterback Demond Williams Jr. leading a favorable schedule.
item.content:encoded:
With Big Ten Media Days wrapping up on Thursday, talking season is officially in the books, and if I may be so bold, thank GOD!

Now we can finally look ahead to the start of college football season, and with that, the picture of 2026 as a whole starts to come into focus.

Speaking of the Big Ten, after looking through the conference's predicted order of finish, I have zeroed in on one dark horse that my shock a ton of people this coming season.

ONE OF THESE EIGHT COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS WILL BE HOISTING THE NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP TROPHY IN 2026

I have been seeing the USC Trojans getting a lot of love as a "sleeper" in the Big Ten conference, and while I really like how 2026 is shaping up for Lincoln Riley and the Men of Troy, they were picked to finish fourth by the media.

I wanted something a little more exciting, and after scrolling a little deeper down the list of teams, I think I may have found my Big Ten sleeper.

All the way down at seventh – not a doormat but certainly not a favorite either – you'll find the Washington Huskies, and I absolutely love what they have going on heading into the season.

INDIANA'S CURT CIGNETTI ROASTS THE SEC AS ESPN STARTS THEIR PROMOTIONAL CAMPAIGN ALREADY: 'WE DON'T WHINE'

For Washington, it starts at the top with head coach Jedd Fisch.

This might be my bias showing, but Fisch was my top pick for the Florida Gators when it became obvious that Lane Kiffin was heading elsewhere. I believe he's one hell of a coach, but the numbers back this up, as well.

Fisch's previous stop before arriving in Seattle was with the Arizona Wildcats, and in year one he inherited a mess of a program, bottoming out at 1-11.

INDIANA COACH CURT CIGNETTI BECOMES UNSTOPPABLE THANKS TO LATEST DEVELOPMENT ON RECRUITING TRAIL

Year two was appreciably better at 5-7, but still nothing to write home about.

In year three, however, Fisch and the Wildcats were the talk of college football, shocking everyone with a 10-3 record and putting players like QB Noah Fifita and wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan on the map.

Surprisingly, Fisch didn't stick around for another year with Fifita and McMillan in Tucson, opting to take over for the newly departed Kalen DeBoer at Washington.

The cupboard was left pretty bare for Fisch when he touched down in the Pacific Northwest, as the new Huskies head coach had to replace 20 of his 22 starters from the team that went to the national championship game just a season prior.

Fisch showed his chops once again, guiding the Huskies to a 6-7 record and a berth in the Sun Bowl despite having to patch together an entire team from scratch.

After a 9-4 season and a bowl win in 2025, it's safe to see why I'm so optimistic about the Huskies given Fisch's track record of ascending each subsequent season.

Washington didn't take a ton of players in the transfer portal, and while some might view that as a negative, I think it's a sign of things stabilizing for the team.

The Huskies rank in the top 15 nationally in returning production at 65%, just a tick under Oregon and UCLA for tops in the Big Ten and certainly a far cry from his first season in Seattle.

The biggest reason for optimism among those returning starters is quarterback Demond Williams Jr.

After spot duty and a few starts in 2024, Williams blossomed into a legitimate threat both through the air and on the ground and was one of the most coveted players in the transfer portal before he opted to return to Washington for his junior year.

Other talented returning starters include offensive tackle Drew Azzopardi and safety Alex McLaughlin, both of whom are generating plenty of buzz in the preseason.

The schedule sets up very nicely for the Huskies, too, as they play five of their first six games within the friendly confines of Husky Stadium and won't leave the Pacific Time Zone until mid-October.

They also avoid Ohio State and Michigan while they get both Indiana and Penn State at home this year.

If you need a Big Ten darkhorse to ride with in 2026, I suggest you look no further than the Washington Huskies.

They have the coaching, the returning production at key positions, and the schedule to be a real threat this coming season.

Buy stock in Fisch and company now, because it won't be getting any cheaper.

item.title: Smithsonian America 250 exhibit features 3x more liberal items than conservative ones
item.description: The Smithsonian's America 250th anniversary exhibit features nearly two dozen items for liberal causes but just seven representing conservatism.
item.content:encoded:
A Smithsonian exhibit designed to commemorate America’s 250th birthday displays numerous objects linked to key points in the nation’s history, though it provides relatively little representation of Christianity or conservatism despite ample coverage for LGBT rights and racial justice movements, among other liberal causes, a Fox News Digital review of the exhibit's online catalog found.

In Pursuit of Life, Liberty & Happiness is an exhibit curated by the Smithsonian Institution with the aim of displaying 250 objects that help to tell the story of America from the 1700s to the present. Among these objects are historically significant items, such as a compass from the 1806 Lewis and Clark expedition, a dress belonging to Dolly Madison, Abraham Lincoln’s hat and the desk the Declaration of Independence was written on.

Also included in the exhibit, according to an online catalog published by the Smithsonian, are a number of objects with clear ties to modern liberal politics, such as a pink "p-ssy hat" worn by a participant of the 2017 Women's March, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s gavel, monarch butterfly wings worn by an illegal immigrant activist and a typewriter belonging to liberal writer Maya Angelou.

Next to Angelou’s typewriter is a picture of a 1970s drag queen "wearing an off-the-shoulder shimmery gown," according to a visual description of the exhibit published by the Smithsonian.

TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY

The exhibit’s selections are drawing scrutiny as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans challenge the Smithsonian’s portrayal of American history around the nation’s 250th anniversary.

Fox News Digital reviewed the Smithsonian’s online catalog and grouped objects according to the movements, causes and institutions identified in the museum’s descriptions, finding seven tied to conservative movements, compared with nearly two dozen tied to causes including LGBT rights, abortion access, racial justice, organized labor and Democratic politics.

The apparent domination of liberal causes in an exhibit designed to celebrate the contributions of all Americans to the nation's history could further inflame conservative criticisms of the museum.

While the exhibit examines how left-of-center individuals and movements shaped American history, conservatives have less representation.

Just seven items representing conservative movements — a MAGA hat, a Tea Party placard, a pro-life sign, a dress worn by Melania Trump, a sign opposing the feminist-backed Equal Rights Amendment, a Ronald Reagan campaign T-shirt and a National Rifle Association button — are presented by the Smithsonian, according to its online catalog.

By comparison, the same catalog shows that liberal causes — such as LGBT rights, farm-worker rights, abortion access, racial justice, environmentalism, labor unions and the Democratic Party — collectively have nearly two dozen items representing them.

THE WAR ON AMERICA’S JUDEO-CHRISTIAN ROOTS THREATENS EVERYTHING WE SHARE

Among those, the Smithsonian chose four total items representing the gay rights movement, for example. 

That wasn't far behind the six it curated to represent Christianity, including items from churches and a Bible, per its catalog. Christianity historically was America's dominant faith, influencing nearly all aspects of life, though it has declined in prominence in recent decades.

Even the items representing Christianity, however, include undertones of racial justice. 

A pew from a Black Presbyterian church, for example, is accompanied by a description of its pastor's racial activism. The one Bible on display as part of the exhibit, meanwhile, discusses the owner's anti-slavery sentiments.

Other religions, such as Judaism, with a Seder plate and a Hanukkah lamp, and the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day saints, colloquially known as Mormons, with a plate depicting one of their temples, received representation as well.

Among the LGBT artifacts displayed by the Smithsonian is a red tie that belonged to the late lesbian activist Carmen Vázquez. A description for the item notes that she described it as her "seduction necktie."

"Vázquez was born in Puerto Rico and grew up in New York City. After College, she lived in San Francisco for many years, honing her political understanding of immigrant rights and women’s and public health," the online exhibit description continues. "Her endless energy for LGBTQ+ rights and justice for all, and her work, writing, and speeches ensured the safety and capacity to thrive of countless people across the United States."

LGBTQ PRESS CONFERENCE AT TRACK MEET INVOLVING TRANS ATHLETE DESCENDS INTO CHAOS, POLICE SUMMONED

The online catalog also shows that nearly two-dozen items displayed at the exhibit are related to recent waves of Asian and Latino immigration. Earlier migrant groups such as the Irish, French and Italians, received just one entry each.

One display dedicated to recent immigrants is a soccer ball donated by the founder of the Fugees soccer team for refugee children in Clarkston, Georgia, describing how the group "overcame anti-immigrant backlash."

The Smithsonian did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital. However, comments made by the National Museum of American History's director provide some insight as to why curators made the decisions they did when selecting items for the exhibit.

"How do you structure a commemoration, celebration and time for reflection?" Anthea Hartig, the museum’s director, told British newspaper The Guardian. "What we landed on were those moments where individuals or communities had fought for recognition and advocated for their own sense of identity and self in their role in creating and becoming a part of the United States. But we also wanted to do the playful."

Beyond items of political or ideological significance, the exhibit also makes an effort to showcase historical changes to domestic life, technology and pop culture through the display of everyday objects.

Various household appliances from different points in American history, props from the Star Wars movies, currency spanning hundreds of years, instruments belonging to famous musicians, technological advancements in areas such as video games and telecommunications and sports paraphernalia, like hockey gloves worn during the 1980 "miracle on ice" Olympic match against the Soviet Union, are all on display.

item.title: DAVID MARCUS: America needs a museum for COVID madness
item.description: A proposed Museum of the COVID Lockdowns would memorialize everything from nursing home deaths to remote learning failures and church closures.
item.content:encoded:
Not long after 9/11, I was on St. Mark’s Place in Lower Manhattan when a bartender told me about a makeshift memorial and museum that had been set up nearby. That night, my wife and I walked into a strange, candle-lit, abandoned school filled with newly made paintings, sculptures and even debris. The whole thing was staggeringly beautiful and deeply human.

Watching the entire COVID narrative of 2020 blowing up with the disgrace of Dr. Anthony "Take the Fifth," Fauci, this week, I could not help but think that the COVID lockdowns require their own museum, preferably in Washington, D.C., so that we can finally, truly understand what happened to us.

Despite the bluster of some Republican politicians, it seems clear that there will be little to no legal reckoning for the lies about everything from COVID’s origin, to the efficacy of masking or distancing, to the constant shifting stories about the vaccines. But that doesn't mean we can’t have a physical reckoning.

9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY

In my own vision of the Museum of the COVID Lockdowns, visitors will be given two masks to put on for safety upon entry, and cameras will monitor whether patrons touch their own faces during their visit, with loud sirens announcing violations.

I did a bit of crowdsourcing on social media to see what kinds of exhibits people think belong in this museum. There was no shortage of responses, ranging from hilarious to tragic.

Among the more light-hearted entry suggestions were interpretive dance TikTok videos from teachers and nurses, and photos of socially distant concertgoers sitting in little isolated circles. My favorite suggestion, from a New York liquor distiller, was "A bottle of hand sanitizer my distillery made along with the news article about the FDA trying to fine distillers for making it."

FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

As far as the darker side of the lockdowns go, people came up with a sea of sins, everything from images of grandparents dying alone in nursing homes, to charts showing how many cancer screenings never happened, to the frustration of students locked in pointless remote learning.

At this museum, we will also see the stories of courage and freedom, brave church goers who broke the law to worship, speakeasy New York City bars defying lockdown and even a crazy, freezingly cold, Canadian trucker protest against vaccine mandates.

Such a memorial is needed for the same reason it has been since the pyramids were erected, lest we forget the dead. It was 18th Century philosopher Giambattista Vico who argued that the very term "human," comes from the root word "humando," which means "to bury." Vico says humans are the animals who bury their dead, but we are also the animals who remember them.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

The Museum of the COVID Lockdowns will not just serve as a memorial for those who succumbed to the Chinese virus, but also to those who needlessly perished as a result of ham-fisted overclosures, which, according to former White House COVID Task Force member Dr. Deborah Birx, were overtly politically motivated in blue states.

An advantage that a museum has over retribution is permanence. I can understand those who, after seeing Fauci squirm on the Senate hearing hot seat, or having read the lies he bragged about in his diary, want his last few years spent in jail, but such punishment would fade much faster than the stonework of an institution.

More than anything, a Museum of the COVID Lockdowns would serve as a warning, insurance that we never again are asked to rat out neighbors giving haircuts in backyards, or allow people to go weeks without so much as touching another human being.

What we remember will always be in the past, but the act of remembering will always be in the present, and future generations must know what we allowed to happen so that it never happens again.

In the 25 years since 9/11, I have looked online in vain for any evidence of the impromptu museum that sprang up in the East Village in the face of brutal tragedy. But I know it was real, I know it was organic and I know that it helped.

One-hundred years from now, somewhere on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., our great-grandchildren should have a place to see and understand our folly, to learn what happens when a society trades freedom for the illusion of perfect safety.

The COVID lockdowns of 2020 were the most insane, wrongheaded and inexplicable events of our lifetimes, and it is time that we tell that story, in brick and mortar, so that our progeny do not ever make the same tragic mistakes.
